steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Every opening move does two jobs: it answers what the opponent just did, and it makes a later move possible. We follow both sides of the Najdorf and ask of each early move: *what does this make possible, and what does it cost?* By the end you can build either set-up piece by piece and give a reason for every step. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.text: **When the push gains time.** A push gains time when it attacks a piece and a pawn guards it. Both parts matter. With White's bishop on e2 the pawn on b5 would attack nothing: it is a space move that leaves c6 less covered and costs a tempo. It is good only when it prepares ...b4 against the knight on c3 or ...Bb7 [I]. So before pushing, ask: what does the pawn attack, and what guards it? The next three positions share one base and change one thing each.

steps.text: **A set-up is a list of jobs.** Our opening file names the position after White's bishop goes to e3 the *English Attack* [V]. Its list: a pawn to f3 (guards g4), the queen to d2 (clears the first rank), long castling (king far from the storm) and the g-pawn push (the storm itself). None of these wins anything alone; each makes the next possible. First question: why can the g-pawn not go at once?

steps.text: **Queen out, then the king.** The queen on d2 clears the squares between the king and the rook, and long castling puts the king on c1, far from the g-pawn push. The rook lands on d1, facing the d6 pawn on a half-open file. The cost [I]: Black's pieces (the bishop on e6, a knight heading for c5) now aim at the queenside, and the king faces Black's queenside pawns, so the game becomes a race with the kings on opposite wings.

steps.prompt: Both kings are on opposite wings. Which side do you think wins the race at first glance, and why? A guess is fine: later I report what the engine says, and you can test it yourself in Play.

steps.text: **Black's list.** Black has jobs too. The pawn to e5 takes space and attacks the knight. The bishop goes to e6: it guards d5, where White's knight wants to land, and eyes the white knight on b3. The other bishop comes to e7 and the king castles. Last come the knight to d7 and the pawn to b5 for counter-play. The two bishop moves can come in either order; the next two boards reach the same set-up both ways.

steps.text: **What to remember about the race.** [I] In the English Attack each side's attack uses pawns on the wing where the enemy king stands. The side that makes threats first forces the other to answer. The engine rates the line we stepped through between level and slightly better for White, so neither wing wins by itself [V]. To test it yourself: in your own games, count how often each side's first attack move is a pawn move.

steps.text: **Other ways to set up.** After the same fifth move White has more plans. The bishop to g5 attacks the knight on f6; lesson 4 follows that line move by move. The bishop to e2 prepares short castling and a calm game, and the bishop to c4 aims at f7; lesson 5 compares these sidelines. [I] Each fits a different structure. Here is one board for each.

steps.text: **Which set-up fits which position?** In the English Attack White's own king goes to c1 first, so the g-pawns can advance without exposing it. In the calm Be2 set-up both kings sit behind their pawns, so g4 would loosen White's own king and is not the plan here: the engine rates it clearly worse in that position [V]. [I] Before you borrow a plan, ask where the kings stand.

**Move orders keep or lose options.** At the sixth move our master file shows the bishop to e3 in 2,669 games, the bishop to g5 in 1,589, the bishop to e2 in 1,371, h3 in 1,286 and f3 in 528 [V]. The engine puts five different moves within 15 centipawns at depth 16 [V]. Many roads lead to the same position, and some move orders walk into a trap.

steps.text: **The order lesson.** The bishop can go to e3 before the pawn move or after, but only when the knight is not under attack. After ...e5 the knight must move first. [I] A good habit: before a move order, ask what the opponent's next pawn move attacks.

steps.text: **Recap.** The a6 pawn takes b5 away. ...b5 gains a tempo when it attacks a piece (a bishop on c4 or a4) that the a6 pawn guards; otherwise it is a space move that needs a plan such as ...b4. The English Attack is a chain: f3, queen off d1, long castling, then g4. Black answers: bishop to e6, bishop to e7, castle, then ...b5. Calm set-ups keep both kings together.
